title: Plasmid-mediated colistin resistance gene mcr-1 in Enterobacteriaceae
abstract: BACKGROUND: Colistin is a last-resort polymyxin antibiotic for multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections. METHODS: We screened 1,200 Escherichia coli and Klebsiella isolates from animals and patients for transferable colistin resistance. RESULTS: The plasmid-borne gene mcr-1 encodes a phosphoethanolamine transferase that modifies lipid A, reducing colistin binding to the outer membrane. mcr-1 transferred by conjugation at high frequency. CONCLUSIONS: Horizontal spread of mcr-1 threatens the last line of defence against carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae.

title: NDM-1 metallo-beta-lactamase hydrolyses carbapenems
abstract: New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase 1 (NDM-1) is a zinc-dependent enzyme that hydrolyses almost all beta-lactam antibiotics, including carbapenems. Structural analysis showed that two zinc ions in the active site activate a water molecule that attacks the beta-lactam ring. NDM-1 is not inhibited by clavulanate or avibactam. The blaNDM-1 gene is carried on diverse plasmids, which explains its rapid global dissemination among Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli.

title: Efflux pumps and multidrug resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics. We quantified expression of the MexAB-OprM, MexXY and MexEF-OprN efflux systems in 210 clinical isolates. Overexpression of MexAB-OprM was associated with resistance to beta-lactams and fluoroquinolones, while MexXY overexpression correlated with aminoglycoside resistance. Efflux pump inhibitors restored susceptibility in vitro. Efflux pumps therefore contribute substantially to the multidrug-resistant phenotype of P. aeruginosa.

title: Antibiotic use in livestock and resistance in human pathogens
abstract: We conducted a systematic review of 181 studies on antimicrobial use in food-producing animals. Interventions that restricted antibiotic use in livestock reduced antibiotic-resistant bacteria in animals by about 15 percent. Evidence for transmission to humans was weaker but 24 studies found lower resistance in humans, especially in people with direct contact with animals such as farm workers. Restricting antibiotic use in food animals is associated with lower resistance in both animals and humans.

title: Biofilm-associated antibiotic tolerance
abstract: Bacteria growing in biofilms tolerate antibiotic concentrations up to 1,000 times higher than planktonic cells. Mechanisms include restricted antibiotic penetration through the extracellular polymeric matrix, nutrient gradients that create slow-growing and dormant subpopulations, and the presence of persister cells. Biofilms on medical devices such as catheters are a major cause of chronic and relapsing infections that resist antibiotic therapy.

title: Fluoroquinolone resistance through gyrA and parC mutations
abstract: Fluoroquinolones target DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Sequencing of 340 resistant Escherichia coli isolates found that substitutions in the quinolone resistance-determining region, most often Ser83Leu and Asp87Asn in gyrA and Ser80Ile in parC, accounted for high-level ciprofloxacin resistance. Single gyrA mutations produced low-level resistance, whereas combined gyrA and parC mutations produced clinical resistance.

title: mecA and methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) carries the mecA gene on the staphylococcal cassette chromosome mec (SCCmec). mecA encodes penicillin-binding protein 2a (PBP2a), which has low affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics and continues cell wall synthesis when native PBPs are inhibited. This makes MRSA resistant to nearly all beta-lactams, including methicillin and oxacillin.

title: Vancomycin resistance in enterococci
abstract: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) acquire van gene clusters, most commonly vanA and vanB, carried on transposons. These genes reprogram cell wall synthesis so that peptidoglycan precursors end in D-alanyl-D-lactate instead of D-alanyl-D-alanine, lowering vancomycin binding affinity about 1,000-fold. VRE are a leading cause of hospital-acquired bloodstream infections.

title: Bacteriophage therapy for multidrug-resistant infections
abstract: We report 20 patients with multidrug-resistant bacterial infections treated with personalised bacteriophage therapy under compassionate use. Clinical improvement or eradication was observed in 11 of 20 patients without serious adverse events. Phage resistance emerged in some cases. Bacteriophage therapy is a promising adjunct for multidrug-resistant infections but controlled trials are needed.

title: Hospital antimicrobial stewardship and resistance outcomes
abstract: A meta-analysis of 32 studies found that antibiotic stewardship programmes in hospitals reduced the incidence of infections and colonisation with multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria by 51 percent and with MRSA by 37 percent. Stewardship also reduced Clostridioides difficile infections. Effects were larger when stewardship was combined with infection control measures such as hand hygiene.

title: Ceftazidime-avibactam for carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae
abstract: In a cohort of 137 patients with carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteraemia, treatment with ceftazidime-avibactam was associated with higher clinical success and lower 30-day mortality than colistin-based regimens. Avibactam inhibits KPC and OXA-48 carbapenemases but not metallo-beta-lactamases such as NDM. Resistance to ceftazidime-avibactam emerged through mutations in blaKPC.

title: Hospital wastewater as a reservoir of antibiotic resistance genes
abstract: Metagenomic sequencing of hospital effluent and municipal wastewater showed that hospital wastewater contained higher abundance of carbapenemase genes and mobile genetic elements. Resistance genes persisted through treatment plants into receiving rivers. Hospital wastewater is a hotspot for environmental dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes.

title: Integrons capture antibiotic resistance gene cassettes
abstract: Class 1 integrons are genetic platforms that capture and express gene cassettes through site-specific recombination by the integrase IntI1. Most cassettes in clinical integrons encode resistance to aminoglycosides, trimethoprim and beta-lactams. Integrons are often embedded in transposons and plasmids, combining cassette capture with horizontal transfer between bacteria.

title: Machine learning prediction of antimicrobial resistance from genomes
abstract: We trained gradient-boosted models on 5,000 whole-genome sequences of Klebsiella pneumoniae to predict minimum inhibitory concentrations for 20 antibiotics. Models using k-mer features predicted MICs within one doubling dilution with 92 percent accuracy. Genome-based machine learning can predict antimicrobial resistance faster than phenotypic testing.

title: Fitness cost of resistance plasmids
abstract: Carriage of resistance plasmids frequently imposes a fitness cost, reducing bacterial growth rates in the absence of antibiotics. Across 50 plasmid-host pairs, the median cost was 9 percent. Compensatory mutations in either plasmid or chromosome rapidly reduced this cost, which helps explain why resistance persists after antibiotic use stops.

title: Sub-inhibitory antibiotic concentrations select resistant mutants
abstract: Experimental evolution showed that antibiotic concentrations far below the minimum inhibitory concentration select for resistant Escherichia coli and Salmonella. The minimal selective concentration was as low as one-tenth of the MIC for some antibiotics. Low-level antibiotic pollution in the environment can therefore drive enrichment of resistance.
